history.title: A Church That Traveled Through Time
history.intro:
What you see today in the Eixample… was not born here.
Discover how this Gothic church was moved stone by stone in the 19th century.

content.p: This church was originally part of the Monastery of Santa Maria de Jonqueres in medieval Barcelona.
It stood next to the old city walls, near what is now Plaça Urquinaona.

On December 7, 1942, a beautiful image of the Immaculate Conception — patron saint of the church — created by sculptor Enric Monjo, was placed inside the small Gothic chapel located at the center of the main altar.

items.title: Learn More
items.content:
The Monastery of Jonqueres belonged to the Order of Santiago, a religious and military order founded in the 12th century.

The community arrived in Barcelona from Sabadell and settled in this area of the medieval city.

The nuns of Jonqueres, known as commanders or Santiaguist sisters, mostly came from noble families of Barcelona and nearby territories.

Unlike many other medieval convents, life in the community followed relatively flexible rules. The nuns had private spaces where they lived according to family ties or personal affinities, and young novices were educated within the monastery.

As a unique feature, the Order of Santiago allowed its nuns to marry, although this was uncommon before the 16th century.

For centuries, Jonqueres was one of the most important female monasteries in medieval Barcelona.

content.p: In the 19th century, Barcelona expanded beyond its walls, giving rise to the Eixample district.
To allow this expansion, the old monastery was demolished.

But something extraordinary happened:
between 1869 and 1871, the church was dismantled and rebuilt here, stone by stone.

items.title: Learn More
items.content:
In the 19th century, Barcelona underwent a profound urban and political transformation.

After the demolition of the city walls and the beginning of the Eixample expansion, many historic buildings disappeared to make room for the new city.

This process was reinforced by the Mendizábal confiscations, promoted by the Spanish State, which led to the closure and expropriation of many convents and monasteries.

The Monastery of Jonqueres was condemned to demolition. However, the Commission of Monuments and the Academy of Fine Arts promoted an exceptional decision for the time:

dismantling the church stone by stone and rebuilding it in the new Eixample district.

The main nave was relocated and inaugurated between 1869 and 1871, while the rest of the complex continued to be completed during the following decades.

cloister.title: A Medieval Garden in the City

content.p: The cloister was part of the original Monastery of Jonqueres.
It was relocated and rebuilt between 1869 and 1888, preserving its Gothic structure.
Today, it is one of the most emblematic spaces of the complex: a place of calm in the heart of Barcelona.

items.title: Learn More
items.content:
The cloister was one of the main spaces of monastic life: a place of silence, prayer, and contemplation.

The original cloister of the Monastery of Jonqueres was approximately twice the size of the current one.

During the relocation and reconstruction of the complex in the 19th century, only part of it could be preserved and adapted to the new available space.

Even so, its galleries and original Gothic elements still allow visitors to imagine the scale and beauty of the old medieval monastery.

content.p: The bell tower did not originally belong to this complex.
It comes from the old Church of Sant Miquel and was added in 1879, completing the current building.

items.title: Learn More
items.content:
The bell tower comes from the former Parish Church of Sant Miquel, a medieval church located near today’s Plaça Sant Jaume.

When that church was demolished, its bell tower was preserved and later incorporated into this complex in 1879.

The combination of elements from different historic buildings turned the basilica into a unique architectural ensemble in Barcelona.
